subcategory: code: retrieval-augmented beam search for program optimisation
problem: LLMs struggle to optimise programs out of the box; the best black-box adaptation (dynamic retrieval of slow-fast program pairs by code embedding) makes end-to-end edits and retrieves on surface code similarity.
architecture: Retrieval Augmented Search (RAS): beam search over candidate optimisations; at each step k=8 in-context slow-fast examples are retrieved by 'contextual retrieval' over LLM-generated natural-language descriptions rather than raw code. AEGIS decomposes training pairs into incremental 'atomic edits' with descriptions to make edits smaller and interpretable.
retriever: embedding retrieval (text-embedding-3-large) over LLM-generated descriptions of programs
generator: GPT-4o, Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek 3.2; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on Mercury
knowledge_source: training set of slow-fast program pairs (PIE) and derived atomic-edit database

datasets.name: PIE
datasets.details: slow-fast C++ program pairs from CodeNet, run in the gem5 simulator

key_results: On PIE with Qwen3-Coder, RAS reaches 8.70x mean best speedup vs 4.23x for dynamic retrieval; 9.18x with DeepSeek 3.2.
AEGIS reaches 6.08x with GPT-4o while reducing average edit size by 17% relative to RAS.
On Mercury (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) RAS obtains Beyond@1 87.85 vs 69.26 (No Contextual) and 58.66 for the unoptimised base.
strengths: Shows that retrieving on LLM-generated descriptions beats retrieving on code; ablations isolate search and contextual retrieval.
Correctness checked by test cases and, for a subset, by the CBMC model checker.

limitations.text: Beam search makes both methods computationally more expensive; AEGIS needs extra training-time compute to build the atomic-edit dataset.
Scaling to complex, object-oriented codebases with many components is expected to be challenging.
Formal equivalence checking covers only 10 programs.

title: LLM Program Optimization via Retrieval Augmented Search
